specAnchors.text: describe a DNA molecule as two strands coiled to form a double helix, the strands being linked by a series of paired bases: adenine (A) with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) with guanine (G)

primer.text: Before you can talk mutations or protein synthesis you need the shape of the molecule itself. This note assembles DNA from its parts — two strands, a sugar-phosphate backbone, four bases — and locks in the pairing rule, adenine with thymine and cytosine with guanine, that makes the double helix copyable as a template.

modules.title: The Double Helix and Its Pairing Rule
modules.opening: DNA is the cell's genetic material, a two-stranded polymer wound into a double helix, whose sugar-phosphate backbones are bridged by paired bases obeying one rule: adenine always faces thymine, and cytosine always faces guanine.
keyPoints: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid and sits in the nucleus.
Two strands coil around each other to form the double helix.
Each strand is a sugar-phosphate backbone carrying the bases A, T, G and C.
Complementary pairing links A with T and G with C.
Each half helix acts as a template when copying is needed.

low.restatement: DNA is a two-stranded molecule whose bases click together in fixed couples.
low.analogy: A spiral ladder where each rung is a matching pair: only certain rungs fit.
low.examPointer: Use full base names in written answers, not just the letters.

medium.restatement: The pairing rule is what makes the helix a copying machine: either strand determines its partner exactly.
medium.analogy: A zip whose teeth only close in one combination, so one half predicts the other.
medium.examPointer: Link the template idea to both cell division and protein synthesis.

glossary.definition: Deoxyribonucleic acid, the genetic material held in the nucleus.
The two-stranded coil formed by the DNA molecule.
The fixed rule that adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine.
A strand whose bases dictate exactly which bases join to rebuild its partner.
